strings.FHGSView.3392ce98: On August 19, 2026, the Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD) and the Department of City Planning (DCP) released the draft of the city\u{2019}s first Fair Housing Growth Strategy, required by Local Law 167 of 2023. It estimates how much housing New York City needs over the next ten years and sets a non-binding 2030 housing target for every one of the 59 community districts, including Brooklyn Community District 6.

strings.FHGSView.493ba416: Chapter 4 names the obstacles to fair housing and the strategies to overcome them, under three headings.
strings.FHGSView.6c20a7c6: The report has three parts. The **Housing Needs Assessment** puts the city\u{2019}s ten-year need at 700,000 homes: 290,000 to address today\u{2019}s shortage, 240,000 for population growth and 170,000 for a healthier housing market. The **Housing Production Targets** set a five-year goal of 350,000 new homes by 2030, half the ten-year need, with 85,000 affordable, 25,500 deeply affordable and 12,750 for households experiencing homelessness, plus 100,000 homes preserved, and split the new construction across the 59 community districts. The **Strategic Equity Framework** sets out 18 strategies under three headings: mobility, stability and neighborhood equity.
strings.FHGSView.80cd46d1: {0} new homes is {1} of the homes in the district in 2025. By size of goal it ranks {2} of {3} in {4} and {5} of {6} citywide.
strings.FHGSView.b8006b4c: \u{201C}Goal vs. 2025\u{201D} is the five-year goal divided by homes in 2025, from the report\u{2019}s own columns. LAA is a Limited Affordability Area.
strings.FHGSView.bc4bedbc: District targets are set in four steps: group districts by how much housing they added from 2016 to 2025, give each group a five-year growth rate, raise the rate 25% in Limited Affordability Areas, then take 25% of the total as affordable, 30% of that as deeply affordable and 50% of that for homeless households. The report is a separate thing from the Affordable Housing Fast Track the voters approved in 2025, which applies to 12 districts. HPD and DCP say the final strategy will be released in October 2026 and updated every five years.

strings.GowanusFeature.43907c19: Zoning determines what can legally be built on specific pieces of land. A rezoning changes what is and isn't allowed. In New York City, doing that requires an applicant to go through the Universal Land Use Review Process, commonly known as ULURP. In the case of the Gowanus rezoning, New York City was the applicant, and it resulted in changing more than 80 blocks that were mostly industrial into a new mixed-use district with over 9,000 units of housing, including around 3,000 permanently affordable units, along with more than 6 acres of new open space, parkland, and space for artists and more.

strings.GowanusFeature.eecad7ad: The Gowanus neighborhood went through a major rezoning in 2021, one of the largest in New York City history, covering roughly 82 blocks. CB6 helped shape that outcome in a real and substantive way. After years of advocacy, letters, meetings, and public process alongside many across the community, the final rezoning included major outcomes that did not happen by accident: net 100 percent affordable housing at Public Place, a commitment to net zero CSO, and capital funding for NYCHA. That last point mattered in particular. At the outset, we were told rezoning-linked NYCHA funding could not happen. CB6, the Gowanus Neighborhood Coalition for Justice, many others across the community, and the City Council, with Brad Lander leading in a rare example of member deference being used to make a land use action better, did not accept that answer. They kept pushing, and eventually it became reality. When the City and City Council finalized their Points of Agreement in November 2021, the overlap with what CB6 and the broader community had been calling for was hard to miss.

Sammy's Law, which gave New York City the authority to lower speed limits below the state minimum, was named for a child killed by a speeding driver in this district. strings.UOLHousing.c57b218f: **Only two things decide eligibility: headcount and total counted income.** Who earns it does not matter. Two adults earning $30,000 each and one adult earning $60,000 with a baby are the same household to HPD: 2 people, $60,000. Both qualify from the same AMI band. But that same $60,000 with only one person in the household qualifies from a higher band, because the limits rise with household size.
strings.UOLHousing.c812a8e3: **Unit size follows occupancy standards.** Every open lottery uses the same ranges: studio 1–2 people, 1-bedroom 1–3, 2-bedroom 2–5, 3-bedroom 3–7, 4-bedroom 4–9. These are the household-size ranges printed in each lottery's own Available Units table on Housing Connect. They set who *may* apply for a size, not who must: a household of three can apply for a 1-bedroom, 2-bedroom or 3-bedroom. HPD sets these in its Marketing Handbook and revised them upward by one person per unit size, so older published ranges may differ.

strings.WeatherView.364e08bd: Parts of CB6, especially Red Hook, the Columbia Waterfront, and the Gowanus Canal area, face flood risk. Coastal flooding comes from the harbor: storm surge and rising high tides. Rainfall flooding happens when a downpour drops water faster than the sewers can carry it away, and can happen blocks from the water.
